newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: FEATURE-Crime eclipses peace in minds of Guatemalans.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Crime eclipses peace in minds of Guatemalans.

text.p: Guatemala's government and leftist rebels are engaged in historic negotiations to end a 36-year civil war but the average citizen is more interested in protecting his car stereo than following the peace talks.

A wave of car thefts, kidnappings and lynchings that began early this year has eclipsed talks that should lead to the ratification of a definitive peace treaty by December. Government and guerrilla negotiators in September signed a landmark agreement to reduce the powerful army by one-third and limit its postwar role. Now they are working on terms for exiled guerrillas to return to normal life.
But the end of war does not mean the end of violence.

Since the early 1960s Guatemala has endured extrajudicial executions and massacres as military, paramilitary or police forces carried out repressive campaigns against leftists, political enemies and suspected guerrillas. The war left 100,000 dead, an estimated 40,000 missing and a tradition of threats and bloodshed in politics.

"It's a culture of violence that the country has lived in during so many years, related to the conflict and the excesses on both sides," said Interior Minister Rodolfo Mendoza, who has overseen the nation's police and prisons since January.

He told Reuters a crime wave was not unusual after years of repressive military governments. "When a country leaves behind an authoritarian regime undoubtedly there's an increase in the indices of violence and deliquency."

Many wartime crimes have gone unpunished. Such impunity, along with threats and corruption, have weakened the justice system, creating a ripe climate for the growth in organised crime, which is Guatemala's biggest security problem. Rights of criminals to due process and a presumption of innocence are distant ideals to most Guatemalans.
"The real solution is that the cycle of justice function effectively," Mendoza said.

Intensive internationally funded training programmes for judges, prosecutors and police should begin to bring about change, but in the meantime Guatemalans, frustrated by ineffective courts, have resorted to lynchings. Enraged mobs have killed up to an estimated 31 suspected thieves and murderers this year.
"Guatemala has a sad history of people taking justice into their own hands," Mendoza said. "In the past much of that was confused with the armed confrontation we were immersed in."
Although the public's No. 1 concern is crime, according to newspaper polls, arrests, anti-corruption campaigns and training have begun to brighten the law-enforcement picture.

The National Police force has arrested 20 bands of kidnappers this year and abductions for ransom have come down. The government's much-publicised commitment to fighting crime has made Guatemalans more willing to provide information, especially to an anonymous hotline for tips on kidnappings.

Purges of corrupt police officers also have encouraged Guatemalans to collaborate more with authorities. Police officers and former policemen are widely believed to be involved with kidnappings and other organised crime.

Under a new training programme, the government hopes to beef up the seriously understaffed police force. Now 7,000 police officers serve a population of 10.5 million but the government aims to triple that by 1999. Spain is providing financial and technical support for speciality training for investigators.
"It's an ambitions programme," the minister said. "Within a period of three or four years we should count with a very different police force than what we have at the moment."

The government cannot rush in new police officers while trying to institute good training programmes, so the police have called on the army for help in patrolling neighbourhoods in the capital in recent months. This has allowed the police to set up roadblocks on highways leaving the capital and reduce car thefts from 25 a day in 1995 to 13 daily in September.
